entries.10:38: But if he is doing those works, believe the works even if you can't believe him yet, so you'll know the Father is in him and he is in the Father. It means the evidence was there for anyone willing to look.
entries.10:39: They tried again to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. It means his time had not yet come, and no one could take him before then.
entries.10:40: He went back across the Jordan to where John had first baptized, and stayed there a while. It means he withdrew to a quieter place rather than forcing a confrontation.
entries.10:41: Many people came to him and said John never did any miracles, but everything John said about this man was true. It means a faithful witness was confirmed, even without signs.
entries.10:42: Many people in that place came to believe in Jesus. It shows that hearing about him can lead someone to trust him, just as it did for them.
entries.11:1: A man named Lazarus was sick, and he lived in Bethany with his sisters Mary and Martha. This tells the reader that the story is about real people in a real place.
entries.11:2: This Mary is the same woman who later poured expensive perfume on Jesus and dried his feet with her hair. The writer adds this so readers can identify which Mary he means.
entries.11:3: The sisters sent a message to Jesus saying that his close friend was sick. They expected him to care and to come.
entries.11:4: Jesus said this sickness would not end in death but would show God's glory and bring glory to God's Son. The reader learns that even bad situations can serve a bigger purpose.
entries.11:5: Jesus loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus. His love for them is stated plainly before he does anything.
entries.11:6: Even after hearing Lazarus was sick, Jesus stayed where he was for two more days. His delay was deliberate, not neglect.
entries.11:7: After the two days, Jesus told his disciples they should go back to Judea. He was ready to move toward the danger.
entries.11:8: The disciples reminded Jesus that people there had recently tried to stone him, and they wondered why he would return. They were afraid for his safety.
entries.11:9: Jesus answered with a picture of daylight: there are twelve hours in a day, and a person walking in daylight does not stumble because he can see. He was saying that while his time to work lasts, he can walk safely.
entries.11:10: A person walking at night stumbles because he has no light. Jesus was saying that working outside God's timing is what brings danger.
entries.11:11: Jesus told them their friend Lazarus was asleep and that he was going to wake him. He used sleep as a picture for death.
entries.11:12: The disciples took him literally and thought Lazarus was just resting, which they believed meant he would recover. They did not understand what Jesus meant.
entries.11:13: Jesus was really talking about Lazarus's death, but the disciples thought he meant ordinary sleep. The reader is told this so the misunderstanding is clear.
entries.11:14: Jesus then told them plainly that Lazarus had died. He stopped using the picture and spoke directly.
entries.11:15: Jesus said he was glad he was not there, for the disciples' sake, so they would believe. The hard situation was meant to strengthen their faith.
entries.11:16: Thomas told the other disciples they should go too, so they could die with Jesus. He expected the trip to end in death.
entries.11:17: When Jesus arrived, Lazarus had already been buried four days. This makes clear that death was real and not recent.
entries.11:18: Bethany was only about two miles from Jerusalem. This explains why so many people were nearby.
entries.11:19: Many Jewish people had come to Martha and Mary to comfort them about their brother. Grieving was a shared, community event.
entries.11:20: When Martha heard Jesus was coming, she went out to meet him, but Mary stayed in the house. The two sisters responded differently.
entries.11:21: Martha told Jesus that if he had been there, her brother would not have died. She believed his presence could have prevented the death.
entries.11:22: Even so, Martha trusted that whatever Jesus asked of God, God would give him. She still had hope.
entries.11:23: Jesus told her that her brother would rise again. He gave her a promise of life after death.
entries.11:24: Martha understood this as the future resurrection on the last day. She believed it would happen, but later.
entries.11:25: Jesus is resurrection and life, not just the one who arranges them. Death does not get the last word.
entries.11:26: Jesus said that anyone living and believing in him will never truly die, and he asked if she believed this. He was pointing to a life that death cannot end.
entries.11:27: Martha said yes and declared her faith that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, who was promised to come. She put her trust in who he is.
entries.11:28: Martha went back and quietly told Mary that the Teacher had arrived and was asking for her. She shared the news privately.
entries.11:29: When Mary heard this, she got up quickly and went to Jesus. She responded at once.
entries.11:30: Jesus had not yet entered the town but was still where Martha had met him. This explains why Mary went out to him.
entries.11:31: The people comforting Mary saw her get up and leave quickly, so they followed, thinking she was going to the tomb to cry there. They meant to support her.
entries.11:32: Mary fell at Jesus's feet and said that if he had been there, her brother would not have died. She expressed the same grief and belief as Martha.
entries.11:33: When Jesus saw Mary and the people with her weeping, he was deeply moved and troubled in spirit. He did not stay distant from their pain.
entries.11:34: Jesus asked where they had laid Lazarus, and they invited him to come and see. He went toward the place of grief.
entries.11:35: Jesus wept. He genuinely grieved, showing that sorrow is not wrong and that he shares in human pain.
entries.11:36: The people said, See how much Jesus loved Lazarus. His tears showed his love plainly.
entries.11:37: Some wondered why Jesus, who had opened a blind man's eyes, could not have kept his friend from dying. People were questioning and confused.
entries.11:38: Deeply troubled, Jesus came to the tomb, which was a cave with a stone covering the opening. The scene is set for what he will do next.
entries.11:39: Jesus told them to remove the stone, but Martha objected that the body would smell after four days. She was thinking practically about the reality of death.
entries.11:40: Jesus reminded Martha that if she believed, she would see God's glory. He asked her to trust him even when it seemed too late.
entries.11:41: They removed the stone, and Jesus looked up to heaven and thanked the Father for hearing him. He prayed openly before acting.
entries.11:42: Jesus is praying out loud so the crowd can hear and understand that God always listens to him and that God truly sent him. It shows readers that Jesus' power comes from God and is meant to be seen and believed.
entries.11:43: Jesus calls the dead man Lazarus to come out of the tomb by name and in a loud voice. It shows that Jesus has real authority over death and can call someone back to life.
entries.11:44: Lazarus comes out alive but still wrapped in burial cloths, so Jesus tells the people to unwrap him and let him go free. It shows that Jesus brings life, and he uses ordinary people to help complete the work.
entries.11:45: Many people who came to comfort Mary saw what Jesus did and put their trust in him. Seeing Jesus' power at work can lead a person to believe in him.
entries.11:46: Some of the witnesses did not believe but instead reported what happened to the religious leaders. Not everyone who sees something amazing responds with faith; some go along with those who oppose Jesus.
entries.11:47: The religious leaders call a meeting and admit that Jesus is doing many miraculous signs, yet they treat him as a problem. People can see clear evidence of God at work and still resist it.
entries.11:48: The leaders fear that if everyone believes in Jesus, the Romans will crush them and destroy their temple and nation. Their concern is political and self-protective rather than about what is true.
entries.11:49: Caiaphas, the high priest that year, speaks bluntly and tells the others they understand nothing. He steps forward as the one who will push the decision against Jesus.
entries.11:50: Caiaphas argues that it is better for one man to die than for the whole nation to be destroyed. He thinks he is giving practical political advice, but his words carry a deeper meaning he does not realize.
entries.11:51: John explains that Caiaphas, as high priest, unknowingly spoke a true prophecy that Jesus would die for the nation. God can use even the words of an opponent to point to his plan.
entries.11:52: Jesus' death was not only for the Jewish nation but also to bring together God's scattered children from everywhere into one people. His death has a purpose that reaches far beyond one group or place.
entries.11:53: From that day on, the leaders plotted together how to kill Jesus. Their opposition moved from discussion to a settled plan, showing how far people will go to protect their own position.
entries.11:54: Jesus stopped moving about openly and withdrew with his disciples to a town near the wilderness called Ephraim. He knew the danger and chose to stay out of the public eye for a time.
entries.11:55: The Jewish Passover was coming, and many people traveled up to Jerusalem early to purify themselves for the festival. The setting shows the religious importance of the season and the crowds gathering.
entries.11:56: People in the temple courts were looking for Jesus and asking each other whether he would come to the festival. Jesus had become the center of attention and speculation among the crowds.
entries.11:57: The chief priests and Pharisees had ordered anyone who knew where Jesus was to report it so they could arrest him. The leaders were actively hunting him, making the situation dangerous for anyone who helped him.
entries.12:1: Jesus arrived in Bethany six days before Passover, back where he had raised Lazarus from the dead. It reminds us that Jesus really did bring a dead man back to life.
entries.12:2: Friends gave Jesus a dinner, Martha served, and Lazarus sat at the table with him, alive and well. It shows the joy of a home where Jesus is welcomed.
entries.12:3: Mary poured expensive perfume on Jesus' feet and dried them with her hair, filling the house with its scent. It shows her deep love and gratitude toward him.
entries.12:4: Judas Iscariot, the disciple who would later betray Jesus, spoke up. It's a warning that even close followers can have wrong hearts.
entries.12:5: Judas asked why the perfume wasn't sold and the money given to the poor. It sounded generous, but his motives were not good.
entries.12:6: Judas didn't really care about the poor; he was a thief who took money from the group's funds. It warns us that fine-sounding words can hide selfish hearts.
entries.12:7: Jesus told Judas to leave Mary alone and let her keep the perfume for his coming death. He accepted her act of love and pointed ahead to what was coming.
entries.12:8: Jesus said the poor would always be around to help, but he would not be with them much longer. It reminds us to value the time we have with him.
entries.12:9: A large crowd came to Bethany, not only to see Jesus but also to see Lazarus, the man he had raised. News of the miracle drew people in.
entries.12:10: The chief priests even plotted to kill Lazarus. They were willing to destroy evidence of a miracle to protect their position.
entries.12:11: Many people were turning away from the priests and believing in Jesus because of Lazarus. One changed life can lead many others to faith.
entries.12:12: The next day, crowds who had come for the feast heard Jesus was heading to Jerusalem. Excitement was building.
entries.12:13: People waved palm branches and shouted blessings, calling Jesus the King of Israel. They welcomed him as a king, though not in the way he came to be one.
entries.12:14: Jesus found a young donkey and rode it into the city, fulfilling what the Scriptures said. He came as a humble king, not a warrior on a horse.
entries.12:15: The prophecy told God's people not to be afraid because their King was coming, riding on a donkey. Jesus' arrival brings comfort, not fear.
entries.12:16: The disciples didn't understand all this at first, but after Jesus was raised to glory they realized the Scriptures were about him. Some things only make sense later.
entries.12:17: The people who had seen Jesus call Lazarus out of the grave kept telling others about it. Eyewitnesses spread the news of what he had done.
entries.12:18: The crowd went out to meet Jesus because they had heard about the miracle he performed. News of his power drew people to him.
entries.12:19: The Pharisees admitted among themselves that they were getting nowhere because the whole world seemed to be following Jesus. Their opposition was failing.
entries.12:20: Some Greeks who had come to worship at the feast were also there. Even outsiders were drawn toward Jesus.
entries.12:21: These Greeks asked Philip if they could see Jesus. People from far away were seeking him out.
entries.12:22: Philip told Andrew, and together they brought the request to Jesus. It shows how seekers were passed along to Jesus himself.
entries.12:23: Jesus answered that the time had come for the Son of Man to be glorified. He was pointing to his coming death and resurrection.
entries.12:24: Jesus compared himself to a seed that must be buried and die before it can produce a harvest. His death would bring life to many.
entries.12:25: Jesus said that clinging to your own life will cost you it, but letting go of it for his sake keeps it forever. Following him means putting him before yourself.
entries.12:26: Anyone who serves Jesus must follow him and will be with him, and the Father will honor that person. Serving Jesus means staying close to him.
entries.12:27: Jesus admitted his soul was deeply troubled and asked whether he should pray to escape that hour, then affirmed this was exactly why he came. Even Jesus faced inner struggle and chose to do God's will.
entries.12:28: Jesus prayed for the Father's name to be glorified, and a voice from heaven said it had been and would be again. God the Father openly affirmed his Son.
entries.12:29: People who heard the voice said it was thunder or an angel speaking. Not everyone recognized God's voice when they heard it.
entries.12:30: Jesus told the crowd the voice was for their benefit, not his. God's words were meant to strengthen the people's faith.
entries.12:31: Jesus announced that the world was now being judged and its ruler would be cast out. His death would break the power of evil over the world.
entries.12:32: Jesus said that when he was lifted up from the earth, he would draw all people to himself. His death on the cross would become the way people come to him.
entries.12:33: This statement showed what kind of death Jesus would die. He was speaking plainly about being lifted up on a cross.
entries.12:34: The crowd was confused, since they believed the Messiah would live forever, so they asked who this Son of Man was. They couldn't reconcile his words with their expectations.
entries.12:35: Jesus told them the light would only be with them a little longer, so they should walk in it before darkness overtook them. It's a call to act while you still have the chance.
entries.12:36: Jesus urged them to believe in the light while they had it so they could become children of light, then he withdrew from them. Trusting Jesus makes you part of his light.
entries.12:37: Even after all his miracles, many still refused to believe in him. Seeing wonders doesn't guarantee faith.
entries.12:38: This fulfilled Isaiah's words asking who would believe the message and to whom God's power would be revealed. Unbelief was predicted long before.
entries.12:39: Because of this, they were unable to believe, as Isaiah had also said. Their refusal to believe was part of a pattern God had foretold.
entries.12:40: Isaiah said God had blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts so they wouldn't see, understand, and be healed. Persistent rejection of God can leave a person unable to turn back.
entries.12:41: Isaiah saw a vision of God's glory and wrote about it, and John says that glory was actually Jesus. So the Old Testament points forward to Jesus, and reading it can lead you to him.
entries.12:42: Many leaders actually believed in Jesus but kept quiet because they were afraid of being thrown out of the synagogue. Fear of what people will do can keep even sincere believers from speaking openly.
entries.12:43: They cared more about what people thought of them than about what God thought of them. It's a warning to check whose approval you are really living for.
entries.12:44: Jesus calls out that trusting him is really trusting God, who sent him. So coming to Jesus is not a detour from God; it is the way to God.
entries.12:45: Anyone who looks at Jesus is seeing the God who sent him. Jesus shows us plainly what God is like.
entries.12:46: Jesus came into the world like a light so that anyone who believes in him will not stay in darkness. Trusting him brings light and direction to your life.
entries.12:47: Jesus says he did not come to condemn people but to rescue them, so hearing his words and ignoring them is not the end of the story yet. His first purpose toward the world is salvation, not judgment.
entries.12:48: Rejecting Jesus and ignoring his words is not a small thing, because those very words will stand as the standard that judges a person on the last day. What you do with his teaching matters forever.
entries.12:49: Jesus did not make up his message on his own; the Father who sent him told him exactly what to say. So his words carry God's own authority.
entries.12:50: God's command is eternal life, and Jesus speaks only what the Father gives him to say. Listening to Jesus is listening to the words that lead to life.
entries.13:1: Jesus knew his death was near and that he would soon return to God. Even knowing what was coming, he kept loving his followers all the way to the end, and he keeps loving you the same way.
entries.13:2: During the meal, the devil had already planted the idea in Judas's mind to betray Jesus. It reminds us that evil can work quietly in a person's heart before it shows.
entries.13:3: Jesus knew God had given him full authority and that he had come from God and was going back to God. Knowing who he was gave him the freedom to serve humbly.
entries.13:4: Jesus got up from the table, took off his outer robe, and wrapped a towel around himself like a servant. The greatest person there chose to act like the lowest servant.
entries.13:5: He poured water into a basin and washed and dried the disciples' feet, the dirtiest job a servant would do. He served them in a way that cost him dignity.
entries.13:6: When Jesus came to Peter, Peter was shocked and asked if his Lord was really going to wash his feet. It felt wrong to him for the master to serve the student.
entries.13:7: Jesus told Peter he didn't understand now what was happening, but he would understand later. Some things God does only make sense after we've walked through them.
entries.13:8: Peter refused strongly, but Jesus said that without this washing Peter would have no share with him. Accepting Jesus' humble service is necessary to belong to him.
entries.13:9: Peter overcorrected and asked for his hands and head to be washed too. He wanted to be fully clean once he realized what was at stake.
entries.13:10: Jesus explained that a person who has bathed only needs their feet washed to be completely clean. He added that his disciples were clean, though not every one of them.
entries.13:11: Jesus knew who would betray him, which is why he said not all of them were clean. He sees hearts that others cannot see.
entries.13:12: After washing their feet and putting his robe back on, Jesus sat down and asked if they understood what he had just done. He wanted them to think about the meaning, not just the action.
entries.13:13: They called him Master and Lord, and he said they were right to do so. He accepts their respect but then uses his authority to serve.
entries.13:14: Since their Lord and Master washed their feet, they should wash each other's feet too. Those who follow Jesus are called to humble service, not status.
entries.13:15: Jesus said he gave them an example to copy. His life is a pattern for how his followers should treat one another.
entries.13:16: A servant is not greater than his master, and a messenger is not greater than the one who sent him. If Jesus served, his followers cannot expect to be above serving.
entries.13:17: Knowing these things is not enough; you are blessed when you actually do them. The happiness Jesus talks about comes from putting his example into practice.
entries.13:18: Jesus said he was not speaking about all of them, because he knew one would turn against him, fulfilling what Scripture said about a close friend betraying him. Betrayal by someone close is a deep wound.
entries.13:19: Jesus told them ahead of time what would happen so that when it did, they would believe he is who he claimed to be. Foretelling events strengthens their trust.
entries.13:20: Whoever welcomes someone Jesus sends welcomes Jesus himself, and welcoming Jesus means welcoming the Father who sent him. How we receive Jesus' messengers reflects how we receive God.
entries.13:21: Jesus was deeply troubled and openly told them that one of them would betray him. Even knowing the pain ahead, he spoke the truth to those he loved.
entries.13:22: The disciples looked at each other, confused about who he meant. None of them assumed it couldn't be them.
entries.13:23: One disciple, the one Jesus loved dearly, was sitting right next to him, leaning close. Close friendship with Jesus is possible and precious.
entries.13:24: Peter signaled to that close disciple to ask Jesus who the betrayer was. They turned to the one closest to Jesus for an answer.
entries.13:25: Leaning back toward Jesus, that disciple quietly asked him who it was. He went directly to Jesus with the question.
entries.13:26: Jesus answered that it was the one he would give the dipped piece of bread to, and then he handed it to Judas. Even at the moment of betrayal, Jesus reached out to him.
entries.13:27: When Judas took the bread, Satan entered him, and Jesus told him to do what he had to do quickly. Jesus did not stop the betrayal but let it unfold.
entries.13:28: No one at the table understood why Jesus said this to Judas. The others were completely in the dark about what was happening.
entries.13:29: Some thought Judas, who handled the money, was being sent to buy supplies for the feast or to give something to the poor. They assumed the best rather than the worst.
entries.13:30: Judas took the bread and went out at once, and it was night. The darkness outside matched what was happening in his heart.
entries.13:31: After Judas left, Jesus said that now the Son of Man is glorified and God is glorified in him. The cross, which looked like defeat, would actually reveal God's glory.
entries.13:32: If God is glorified in him, God will glorify him in himself, and will do it right away. The Father and the Son honor each other.
entries.13:33: Jesus told his dear followers he would only be with them a little longer, and where he was going they could not come. He was preparing them for his departure.
entries.13:34: Jesus gave them a new command: love one another the same way he has loved them. His kind of love, self-giving and practical, is the mark of his followers.
entries.13:35: Everyone will know you are my disciples by the love you have for each other. Love between his followers is the clearest sign of belonging to Jesus.
entries.13:36: Peter asked where he was going, and Jesus said Peter couldn't follow now but would follow later. Jesus was honest about the timing.
entries.13:37: Peter asked why he couldn't come now and promised to give his life for Jesus. His devotion was sincere but he didn't yet know his own weakness.
entries.13:38: Jesus asked if Peter would really give his life for him, then said that before the rooster crowed Peter would deny him three times. Even the most confident follower can fail, and Jesus knew it in advance.
entries.14:1: Jesus tells his worried friends not to let fear take over their hearts, but to trust God and also to trust him. Whatever is making you anxious, you can bring that fear to God and to Jesus instead of carrying it alone.
entries.14:2: Jesus says God's house has plenty of room, and he is going ahead to prepare a place for his people. This means there is a secure home waiting for you with God, not a cramped or uncertain one.
entries.14:3: Jesus promises that after preparing a place he will come back and bring his people to be with him. The point for you is that being with Jesus is the goal, and he himself guarantees it.
entries.14:4: Jesus says his friends already know where he is going and the way there. He is telling them that the path to God is not hidden from those who follow him.
entries.14:5: Thomas honestly admits he doesn't understand where Jesus is going, so he can't know the way. It shows that honest confusion is allowed, and Jesus answers it rather than scolding it.
entries.14:6: He is the way, the truth and the life. That is a claim to follow, not a theory to debate.
entries.14:7: Jesus says that knowing him is knowing the Father; they are not two separate things to discover. If you know Jesus, you already have real knowledge of God.
entries.14:8: Philip asks Jesus to show them the Father and says that would be enough. He wants a direct display of God, thinking something more is still needed.
entries.14:9: Jesus gently corrects Philip: after all this time with him, seeing Jesus is seeing the Father. You don't need to look past Jesus for another glimpse of God; he shows you what God is like.
entries.14:10: Jesus says he and the Father are completely joined, and the words and works he does come from the Father living in him. What you see and hear in Jesus is God at work, not a solo act.
entries.14:11: Jesus asks his friends to believe he and the Father are one, and says if that's hard, believe because of the works he does. The evidence of his actions is meant to help your faith when words alone feel like a stretch.
entries.14:12: Jesus says those who trust him will do the same works he did, and even greater ones, because he is going to the Father. Your faith connects you to a power bigger than yourself, not a smaller imitation.
entries.14:13: Jesus promises to answer requests made in his name, so that the Father gets the glory. Praying in his name means asking in line with who he is, with the aim of honoring God rather than just getting your way.
entries.14:14: Jesus repeats the promise that he himself will answer requests made in his name. It means you can bring your needs directly to him, not to some distant middleman.
entries.14:15: Jesus ties love for him to keeping his commands. Love here isn't just a feeling; it shows up in how you actually live.
entries.14:16: Jesus says he will ask the Father to send another Helper to be with his people forever. You are not left to manage on your own; God provides ongoing help that doesn't run out.
entries.14:17: Jesus describes the Helper as the Spirit of truth, whom the world can't receive because it doesn't recognize him. But his followers know him because he stays with them and will be in them.
entries.14:18: Jesus promises not to leave his followers orphaned or friendless, because he is coming to them. Even when he seems absent, you are not abandoned.
entries.14:19: Jesus says the world will soon stop seeing him, but his followers will see him and live because he lives. His life becomes the source of their life, even through death.
entries.14:20: Jesus says that in that coming day his followers will understand the close connection between him, the Father, and them. The relationships that seem confusing now will become clear.
entries.14:21: Jesus says whoever has his commands and keeps them is the one who loves him, and such a person will be loved by the Father and will see Jesus clearly. Obedience is the visible shape of real love.
entries.14:22: Judas (not the betrayer) asks how Jesus will show himself clearly to his followers and not to the world. He is puzzled about why everyone won't get the same visible reveal.
entries.14:23: Jesus answers that anyone who loves him will keep his words, and then he and the Father will come and make their home with that person. God's presence isn't a distant visit; it's a dwelling with those who love him.
entries.14:24: Jesus says the one who doesn't love him doesn't keep his words, and the message he speaks isn't his own but comes from the Father who sent him. Rejecting his words is rejecting the One who sent him.
entries.14:25: Jesus notes that he has said all this while still present with them. He is preparing them in advance for what is coming.
entries.14:26: Jesus promises the Father will send the Holy Spirit in his name to teach them everything and remind them of all he said. You are not expected to remember or figure out everything alone; God's Spirit helps you understand.
entries.14:27: His peace is not the kind the world gives, which depends on circumstances. You can be steady while things are not.
entries.14:28: Jesus reminds them he is going away and coming back, and says they should be glad because he is going to the Father, who is greater than he is. His departure isn't a loss for them but a step toward something better.
entries.14:29: Jesus tells them ahead of time so that when it happens they will believe. Forewarning is meant to strengthen faith, not just satisfy curiosity.
entries.14:30: Jesus says he won't talk much longer because the ruler of this world is coming, though that ruler has no hold on him. Evil may press in, but it has no claim on Jesus.
entries.14:31: Jesus says this is happening so the world can see he loves the Father and does what the Father commands, then tells them to get up and go. His obedience is public evidence of his love, and following him means actually moving forward.
entries.15:1: Jesus compares himself to a vine and God the Father to the gardener who tends it. This means your spiritual life depends on staying connected to Jesus, who is the source of it.
entries.15:2: God removes branches that bear no fruit and prunes the fruitful ones so they produce even more. This means God works in your life to cut away what holds you back and help you grow.
entries.15:3: Jesus says his followers are already made clean by the teaching he gave them. This means the words of Jesus have a cleansing effect on your life when you take them in.
entries.15:4: A branch can't bear fruit unless it stays attached to the vine, and neither can you unless you remain in Jesus. This means you need an ongoing, daily connection with Jesus to live the way he intends.
entries.15:5: Branches live by staying attached to the vine. Fruit comes from staying close, not from trying harder.
entries.15:6: A person who doesn't remain in Jesus is like a dried-up branch that gets thrown away and burned. This means cutting yourself off from Jesus leads to spiritual death and loss.
entries.15:7: If you remain in Jesus and his words remain in you, you can ask for anything and it will be done. This means prayer becomes powerful when your life is deeply shaped by Jesus' teaching.
entries.15:8: Bearing much fruit brings glory to God and shows you are truly Jesus' disciple. This means the visible results of your life honor God and prove your faith is real.
entries.15:9: Just as the Father loves Jesus, Jesus loves you, and he tells you to stay in that love. This means you are deeply loved and should make your home in that love.
entries.15:10: Keeping Jesus' commands keeps you in his love, just as he kept the Father's commands and stayed in his love. This means obedience is the way you stay close to Jesus.
entries.15:11: Jesus says all this so his joy can be in you and your joy can be full. This means his teaching is meant to give you complete, lasting joy, not to weigh you down.
entries.15:12: Jesus commands his followers to love each other the same way he has loved them. This means your love for other believers should mirror the love Jesus showed you.
entries.15:13: The greatest love a person can show is to give up their life for their friends. This means sacrificial love, putting others before yourself even at great cost, is the highest kind.
entries.15:14: Jesus calls you his friend if you do what he commands. This means obedience to Jesus is what marks a close, friendly relationship with him.
entries.15:15: Jesus no longer calls his followers servants but friends, because he has shared with them everything the Father told him. This means you are trusted with real understanding of God's plans, not kept in the dark.
entries.15:16: You didn't choose Jesus; he chose you and appointed you to go and bear lasting fruit, so the Father will give you whatever you ask in his name. This means your purpose comes from his choice of you, and your prayers are backed by that calling.
entries.15:17: Jesus repeats his command that his followers love one another. This means loving each other is central, not optional, for his people.
entries.15:18: If the world hates you, remember it hated Jesus first. This means opposition to your faith is normal and you shouldn't be surprised or discouraged by it.
entries.15:19: The world loves its own, but because Jesus chose you out of the world, the world hates you. This means being different from the world around you will cost you acceptance.
entries.15:20: A servant isn't greater than his master, so if people persecuted Jesus they will persecute you, and if they kept his word they will keep yours. This means expect the same treatment Jesus got, both good and bad.
entries.15:21: People will treat you this way because of Jesus' name, since they don't know the one who sent him. This means hostility toward you is really rooted in not knowing God.
entries.15:22: If Jesus hadn't come and taught them, they wouldn't be guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse. This means hearing the truth makes you responsible for how you respond to it.
entries.15:23: Anyone who hates Jesus also hates the Father. This means rejecting Jesus is rejecting God himself; you can't have one without the other.
entries.15:24: If Jesus hadn't done miracles no one else ever did, they wouldn't be guilty, but now they have seen and still hated both him and the Father. This means seeing clear evidence and still rejecting it leaves you without excuse.
entries.15:25: This happened to fulfill what was written in their law: they hated Jesus for no reason. This means the rejection of Jesus was predicted and wasn't caused by anything he did wrong.
entries.15:26: When the Helper comes, the Spirit of truth sent from the Father, he will testify about Jesus. This means the Holy Spirit's job is to confirm and reveal who Jesus really is.
entries.15:27: Jesus' followers will also testify because they were with him from the beginning. This means firsthand experience of Jesus makes you a witness, and the Spirit works alongside that testimony.
entries.16:1: Jesus warned his followers ahead of time so that when hard times came, their faith would not be shaken. It means you can hold on to your trust in him even when trouble comes.
entries.16:2: Jesus said his followers would be thrown out of their places of worship, and some would even be killed by people who believed they were serving God. It means you should not be surprised when doing right brings opposition.
entries.16:3: People would do these things because they did not really know God the Father or Jesus. It means that harmful actions can come from people who are sincerely mistaken about God.
entries.16:4: Jesus told them these things in advance so they would remember his words when it happened. It means remembering what Jesus said can steady you when life gets hard.
entries.16:5: Jesus was about to return to the Father who sent him, yet none of his disciples asked where he was going. It means we can be so focused on our own sadness that we miss what God is doing.
entries.16:6: The disciples were filled with grief because of what Jesus had just told them. It means Jesus sees and understands your sorrow, even when you cannot put it into words.
entries.16:7: Jesus said it was actually better for them that he leave, because then the Helper, the Holy Spirit, would come to them. It means some good things can only come after a painful goodbye.
entries.16:8: When the Holy Spirit comes, he will show the world the truth about sin, about what is right, and about judgment. It means God's Spirit helps people see their need for God clearly.
entries.16:9: The world is shown its sin because people have not believed in Jesus. It means the deepest wrong is refusing to trust the one God sent.
entries.16:10: The Spirit shows what is right because Jesus was going to the Father and would no longer be seen. It means Jesus' return to the Father proves that he was right all along.
entries.16:11: The Spirit shows that judgment is real because the ruler of this world, the devil, has already been judged. It means evil's power is already broken, even if it doesn't always look that way.
entries.16:12: Jesus had much more to teach them, but they were not yet able to handle it. It means God gives you truth in amounts you can actually carry at the time.
entries.16:13: The Spirit of truth will guide them into all truth, speaking only what he hears and telling them what is to come. It means you can trust the Holy Spirit to lead you into what is true.
entries.16:14: The Spirit will bring glory to Jesus by taking what belongs to Jesus and making it known to them. It means the Holy Spirit's work always points you back to Jesus.
entries.16:15: Everything the Father has belongs to Jesus, which is why he said the Spirit would take what is his and make it known. It means Father, Son, and Spirit are completely united in what they give you.
entries.16:16: Jesus said that in a little while they would not see him, and then after a little while they would see him again. It means painful partings from Jesus are temporary, not final.
entries.16:17: The disciples were confused and asked each other what Jesus meant about seeing him again soon and going to the Father. It means it is normal to not understand everything Jesus says at first.
entries.16:18: They kept asking what he meant by "a little while," because his words were unclear to them. It means honest confusion is okay; you don't have to pretend to understand.
entries.16:19: Jesus knew they wanted to ask him about this, so he brought up their question himself. It means Jesus knows your questions before you even ask them.
entries.16:20: Jesus told them they would weep and be sad while the world rejoiced, but their sorrow would turn into joy. It means grief is real, but it is not the end of the story.
entries.16:21: A woman in labor has pain, but once the child is born the joy makes her forget the pain. It means some of the deepest joy comes on the other side of pain.
entries.16:22: They were sad then, but Jesus would see them again and their joy would be permanent. It means the joy Jesus gives cannot be taken away by anyone.
entries.16:23: On that day they would not need to ask him questions, because whatever they asked the Father in his name would be given. It means you can bring your requests straight to God because of Jesus.
entries.16:24: They had not yet asked for anything in Jesus' name, and he told them to ask so their joy would be complete. It means prayer is meant to fill you with joy, not just get answers.
entries.16:25: Jesus had been speaking in figures of speech, but a time was coming when he would tell them about the Father plainly. It means understanding grows over time; clearer light is coming.
entries.16:26: In that day they would ask in Jesus' name, and he said he would not need to plead with the Father for them. It means you can go to the Father directly, confident of welcome.
entries.16:27: The Father himself loves them because they loved Jesus and believed he came from God. It means God's love for you is personal, not something you have to earn through someone else.
entries.16:28: Jesus came from the Father into the world, and he was going to leave the world and return to the Father. It means Jesus' whole story, from heaven to earth and back, is for your sake.
entries.16:29: The disciples said that now he was speaking plainly and not in figures of speech. It means it is a relief when truth finally clicks and becomes clear.
entries.16:30: They were now sure he knew all things and did not need anyone to question him, and they believed he came from God. It means real faith grows as you see who Jesus really is.
entries.16:31: Jesus asked them, "Do you believe now?" It means Jesus invites you to be honest about the strength of your faith.
entries.16:32: Jesus warned that a time was coming, already near, when they would all scatter and leave him alone, yet the Father was with him. It means even when everyone else leaves, God stays with you.
entries.16:33: Trouble is promised, and so is his victory over it. You can have peace in the middle of it.
entries.17:1: Jesus finishes speaking and looks up to pray. He tells God the moment has arrived for him to be honored, so that God will be honored through him.
entries.17:2: God gave Jesus power over every person so he could give lasting life to everyone God entrusted to him. Your life with God comes as a gift through Jesus.
entries.17:3: This lasting life means truly knowing the only real God and knowing Jesus, the one God sent. Knowing God isn't just information; it's a relationship.
entries.17:4: Jesus says he brought God honor on earth by finishing the task God gave him. God values faithful completion of what he asks of us.
entries.17:5: Jesus asks to return to the honor he shared with God before the world existed. He is claiming to have been with God from the very beginning.
entries.17:6: Jesus made God known to the people God gave him from the world. They belonged to God, God gave them to Jesus, and they have held on to God's message.
entries.17:7: Jesus' followers now understand that everything he has comes from God. They recognize his source and trust him.
entries.17:8: Jesus passed on to them the words God gave him, and they accepted them. They became convinced Jesus came from God and believed God sent him.
entries.17:9: Jesus prays specifically for his followers, not for the world in general, because they belong to God. He focuses his prayer on those entrusted to him.
entries.17:10: Everything that belongs to Jesus belongs to God, and the reverse is also true. Jesus says he is honored in his followers.
entries.17:11: Jesus is about to leave the world, but his followers remain in it. He asks God to protect them and keep them united, just as he and God are one.
entries.17:12: While Jesus was with them, he protected them and none was lost except the one destined for ruin, fulfilling what Scripture said. Jesus guarded those given to him.
entries.17:13: Jesus says these things while still in the world so his followers can share his complete joy. His words are meant to fill them with gladness.
entries.17:14: Jesus gave them God's message, and the world hates them because they don't fit its ways, just as Jesus didn't. Following Jesus can bring rejection.
entries.17:15: Jesus doesn't ask God to remove them from the world but to protect them from the evil one. God keeps his people safe while they live in a hostile world.
entries.17:16: Jesus' followers don't belong to the world's system any more than he did. Their true home and loyalty lie elsewhere.
entries.17:17: Jesus asks God to set them apart as holy through the truth, and God's word is that truth. God's word shapes and purifies his people.
entries.17:18: Just as God sent Jesus into the world, Jesus sends his followers into the world. They are sent with a mission, not to hide away.
entries.17:19: Jesus dedicates himself fully to God's purpose so his followers can also be truly set apart. His commitment makes their holiness possible.
entries.17:20: Jesus prays not only for his current followers but for everyone who will believe in him through their message. That includes believers today.
entries.17:21: Jesus prays that all his followers will be united, just as he and God are united, so the world will believe God sent him. Their unity is a sign to others.
entries.17:22: Jesus shares with his followers the honor God gave him so they can be one, just as he and God are one. Unity comes as a gift from him.
entries.17:23: Jesus is in them and God is in him, making them completely one, so everyone can see God sent him and loves them as he loves Jesus.
entries.17:24: Jesus wants those given to him to be with him where he is, so they can see his honor, given because God loved him before the world began. He longs for his followers to be with him forever.
entries.17:25: Jesus calls God righteous and says he knows God, though the world does not, and his followers know God sent him. Knowing God is possible through Jesus.
entries.17:26: Jesus has made God known to them and will keep doing so, so God's love for him can be in them and he can be in them. God's love lives inside his followers.
entries.18:1: Jesus finished praying and led his disciples across a stream to a garden where they often met. Even knowing trouble was coming, he went forward rather than running away.
entries.18:2: Judas, the disciple who betrayed him, knew this spot because Jesus often gathered there with his followers. Familiar places can become places of danger when someone turns against you.
entries.18:3: Judas arrived with soldiers and temple guards carrying weapons and lights. The religious leaders sent a crowd to arrest Jesus as if he were a dangerous criminal.
entries.18:4: Jesus knew exactly what was about to happen, yet he stepped forward and asked the crowd who they wanted. He faced his arrest calmly instead of hiding.
entries.18:5: They said they were looking for Jesus from Nazareth, and he answered plainly that he was the one. Judas stood right there with the crowd that had come to seize him.
entries.18:6: When Jesus said who he was, the men backed away and fell to the ground. Even his simple words carried power that made an armed crowd stumble.
entries.18:7: Jesus asked them again who they were looking for, and they gave the same answer. He made them say clearly whom they had come to arrest.
entries.18:8: Jesus told them again that he was the one they wanted and asked them to let his friends go. He protected his disciples even while giving himself up.
entries.18:9: This happened so that what Jesus had said earlier would come true, that he had kept safe everyone the Father gave him. His care for his followers held even in his arrest.
entries.18:10: Peter pulled out a sword and struck the high priest's servant, cutting off his ear. He tried to fight with violence, but that was not the way Jesus wanted.
entries.18:11: Jesus told Peter to put the sword away and asked whether he should refuse the suffering the Father had given him. Jesus chose to accept God's plan rather than fight it.
entries.18:12: The soldiers, their captain, and the temple guards arrested Jesus and tied him up. The one who had done nothing wrong was treated like a criminal.
entries.18:13: They took Jesus first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. The questioning began with the man who held real influence behind the office.
entries.18:14: Caiaphas was the one who had told the Jewish leaders it was better for one man to die for the people. His words now came true in a way he never intended.
entries.18:15: Peter followed Jesus along with another disciple who was known to the high priest, and that disciple went inside with Jesus. Peter came close, but not all the way.
entries.18:16: Peter was left outside the door until the other disciple spoke to the servant girl and brought him in. A friend helped him get in, but danger was waiting inside.
entries.18:17: The servant girl at the door asked Peter if he was one of Jesus' disciples, and he said he was not. The first of his denials came from a simple question.
entries.18:18: It was cold, so the servants and guards made a fire and stood warming themselves, and Peter joined them. He stood among Jesus' enemies, trying to look like he belonged.
entries.18:19: The high priest questioned Jesus about his followers and his teaching. The leaders were looking for something to use against him.
entries.18:20: Jesus said he had taught openly in synagogues and the temple where everyone could hear, and had said nothing in secret. His message was public, not hidden or plotted.
entries.18:21: Jesus asked why they were questioning him and said to ask the people who had heard him, since they knew what he taught. He pointed to many witnesses instead of defending himself.
entries.18:22: One of the guards slapped Jesus and accused him of disrespecting the high priest. He was struck for giving a truthful answer.
entries.18:23: Jesus asked them to point out anything wrong he had said, and if he had spoken the truth, why he was being struck. He appealed to what was fair even while being treated unfairly.
entries.18:24: Annas sent Jesus, still tied up, to Caiaphas the high priest. The night of questioning and moving from one leader to another went on.
entries.18:25: Peter was still by the fire, and people asked again if he was one of Jesus' disciples, and he denied it. The pressure wore him down and he denied his friend a second time.
entries.18:26: A servant related to the man whose ear Peter had cut off asked if he had seen Peter in the garden with Jesus. Someone who could recognize him spoke up.
entries.18:27: Peter denied it a third time, and right away a rooster crowed. His failure was complete, just as Jesus had warned.
entries.18:28: They led Jesus from Caiaphas to the Roman governor's headquarters early in the morning, but the leaders stayed outside to avoid becoming unclean for Passover. They were careful about ritual purity while handing over an innocent man.
entries.18:29: Pilate came out to them and asked what charge they were bringing against Jesus. The Roman governor had to hear the case.
entries.18:30: They answered that if he were not a criminal they would not have brought him. They gave no real evidence, only their own claim.
entries.18:31: Pilate told them to judge him by their own law, but they said they had no right to put anyone to death. They wanted Rome to carry out the execution.
entries.18:32: This happened so that what Jesus had said about the kind of death he would die would come true. Even the legal details worked out as he had foretold.
entries.18:33: Pilate went back inside and asked Jesus directly if he was the King of the Jews. The charge was political, and the governor wanted to know the answer.
entries.18:34: Jesus asked Pilate whether he was asking on his own or repeating what others had said. He wanted to know where the question was really coming from.
entries.18:35: Pilate replied that he was not a Jew and that Jesus' own nation and leaders had handed him over, then asked what he had done. He was trying to find the real reason for the charge.
entries.18:36: Jesus said his kingdom does not come from this world, and if it did, his followers would have fought to keep him from being arrested. His rule is not built on military power.
entries.18:37: Pilate asked if he was a king, and Jesus said he was born and came into the world to speak the truth, and that those who love truth listen to him. His kingship is about truth, not politics.
entries.18:38: Pilate asked what truth is and then went out and told the crowd he found no fault in Jesus. The judge saw no guilt but did not act on it.
entries.18:39: Pilate reminded them of the yearly custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover and asked if they wanted the King of the Jews freed. He offered them a way out.
entries.18:40: They shouted back that they wanted Barabbas, not Jesus, and Barabbas was an outlaw. The crowd chose a criminal over the innocent man.
entries.19:1: Pilate had Jesus flogged, a brutal beating meant to weaken and humiliate him. It shows how far the authorities went to satisfy the crowd even while calling Jesus innocent.
entries.19:2: The soldiers mocked Jesus as a pretend king, dressing him in thorns and a purple robe. Their joke was cruel, but it accidentally pointed to the truth that he really is a king.
entries.19:3: The soldiers kept taunting Jesus and hitting him while pretending to honor him as king. It shows how deeply people can mock someone they don't understand.
entries.19:4: Pilate brought Jesus out and told the crowd he found no guilt in him. He was trying to avoid condemning an innocent man while still pleasing the crowd.
entries.19:5: Pilate presented the beaten, mocked Jesus to the crowd and said, 'Here is the man.' It invites us to look at Jesus in his suffering and see who he really is.
entries.19:6: The religious leaders and guards demanded Jesus be crucified, but Pilate again insisted he found no crime in him. The crowd's anger was louder than the evidence of innocence.
entries.19:7: The leaders claimed their law required Jesus' death because he called himself the Son of God. They turned a claim about who Jesus is into a reason to kill him.
entries.19:8: Pilate became more afraid when he heard Jesus claimed to be the Son of God. He realized this was bigger than an ordinary political dispute.
entries.19:9: Pilate asked Jesus where he came from, but Jesus stayed silent. Sometimes silence is the strongest answer when words would only be twisted.
entries.19:10: Pilate reminded Jesus that he had the power to release or execute him. He was relying on his authority, not realizing it was limited.
entries.19:11: Jesus told Pilate that any power he had was given by God, and that the one who handed Jesus over carried greater guilt. It reminds us that human authority is real but never ultimate.
entries.19:12: Pilate wanted to release Jesus, but the crowd threatened him with losing Caesar's favor. Fear of what people think can push us to do wrong.
entries.19:13: Pilate took his seat as judge in a public place called the Stone Floor. He was about to make a decision he knew was unjust.
entries.19:14: It was the day of preparation for Passover, and Pilate told the crowd, 'Here is your King.' The timing matters, since Passover recalls God rescuing his people.
entries.19:15: The crowd shouted for Jesus to be crucified, and the leaders declared they had no king but Caesar. They rejected their own Messiah to keep peace with Rome.
entries.19:16: Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified, and the soldiers took him away. The innocent man was condemned to satisfy the crowd.
entries.19:17: Jesus carried his own cross to a place called Golgotha, meaning Skull Hill. He walked the road of suffering himself, not from a distance.
entries.19:18: They crucified Jesus between two other men, one on each side. He died among criminals, sharing the shame of the worst kind of execution.
entries.19:19: Pilate had a sign put on the cross reading 'Jesus the Nazarene, the King of the Jews.' The sign told everyone who this crucified man claimed to be.
entries.19:20: Many people saw the sign because the place was near the city, and it was written in three languages. The message about Jesus was made public for everyone to read.
entries.19:21: The religious leaders asked Pilate to change the sign so it wouldn't state that Jesus was the King of the Jews. They wanted to control how people understood what happened.
entries.19:22: Pilate refused to change the sign, saying what he had written would stand. His stubbornness accidentally left the truth about Jesus on display.
entries.19:23: The soldiers divided Jesus' clothes among themselves, but his coat was one piece of cloth with no seam. Even in death, his belongings were taken as spoils.
entries.19:24: The soldiers decided by chance who would get the seamless coat, which fulfilled an old prophecy about the Messiah's clothing. It shows that even small details were under God's plan.
entries.19:25: Several women stood near the cross, including Jesus' mother and Mary Magdalene. They stayed with him in his worst moment when most others had fled.
entries.19:26: Jesus saw his mother and the disciple he loved standing nearby and told her that disciple would be her son. Even while dying, he made sure she would be cared for.
entries.19:27: Jesus told the disciple to treat his mother as his own, and from then on the disciple took her into his home. It shows love expressed in practical action.
entries.19:28: Knowing everything was nearly finished, Jesus said he was thirsty, fulfilling what the Scriptures said. Even his physical suffering was part of the plan.
entries.19:29: Someone put a sponge soaked in sour wine on a stick and held it to Jesus' mouth. It was a small act of relief in the middle of his agony.
entries.19:30: After drinking the wine, Jesus said 'It is finished' and died. His work of salvation was complete, not cut short.
entries.19:31: Because the next day was a special Sabbath, the leaders asked Pilate to break the prisoners' legs and remove the bodies. They were careful about religious rules while ignoring the injustice they had just done.
entries.19:32: The soldiers broke the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus. This was done to speed up death so the bodies could be taken down before the Sabbath.
entries.19:33: When the soldiers came to Jesus, they saw he was already dead, so they didn't break his legs. This matched what Scripture said about the Messiah.
entries.19:34: One soldier pierced Jesus' side with a spear, and blood and water came out. This showed beyond doubt that Jesus had really died.
entries.19:35: The one who saw this testified to it so that others would believe. The eyewitness account is given to help us trust what happened.
entries.19:36: These events fulfilled the Scripture that said none of his bones would be broken. It shows God's plan was carried out down to the smallest detail.
entries.19:37: Another Scripture said people would look on the one they pierced. Even the spear wound pointed back to promises made long before.
entries.19:38: Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple, asked Pilate for Jesus' body and was allowed to take it. He risked his reputation to give Jesus a proper burial.
entries.19:39: Nicodemus, who had first visited Jesus at night, brought a large amount of burial spices. His open act of devotion showed how far he had come.
entries.19:40: They wrapped Jesus' body in linen with the spices, following Jewish burial customs. It was a careful, loving way to honor him in death.
entries.19:41: There was a garden right by the place where Jesus was crucified, and in it a brand-new tomb where no one had ever been buried. This matters because it shows his burial was real and carefully arranged, not a rushed or borrowed afterthought.
entries.19:42: Because it was the day of preparation for the Passover and the tomb was close by, they laid Jesus there. The timing and location made the burial quick and practical, which fits the account of what actually happened.
entries.20:1: Mary Magdalene went to Jesus' tomb very early in the morning and found the stone moved away. This shows her love and devotion, and it sets up the discovery that changed everything.
entries.20:2: Mary ran to tell Peter and the beloved disciple that Jesus' body was gone, assuming someone had taken it. Her panic shows how little anyone expected a resurrection.
entries.20:3: Peter and the other disciple headed straight for the tomb to see for themselves. When something important happens, it's natural to want to check it out personally.
entries.20:4: The two disciples ran together, and the younger one outran Peter to reach the tomb first. It's a small human detail that makes the account feel real and eyewitnessed.
entries.20:5: The disciple looked inside and saw the burial cloths lying there but didn't go in. He was cautious, taking in the scene before acting.
entries.20:6: Peter arrived and went right into the tomb, where he saw the linen wrappings lying on the ground. Peter's boldness shows his character, and the cloths are key evidence.
entries.20:7: The cloth that had covered Jesus' head was folded up separately from the other wrappings. This detail suggests the body wasn't hastily stolen but that something orderly and deliberate had happened.
entries.20:8: The other disciple finally went in, saw the evidence, and believed. Seeing the empty tomb and the cloths was enough to convince him something miraculous had happened.
entries.20:9: Even so, they didn't yet understand from Scripture that Jesus had to rise from the dead. Belief came before full understanding, which is often how faith works.
entries.20:10: The disciples went back home, probably confused and processing what they'd seen. Sometimes you need time to absorb something before you know what to do with it.
entries.20:11: Mary stayed at the tomb crying and looked inside. Her grief kept her there, and her persistence led to the first encounter with the risen Jesus.
entries.20:12: Mary saw two angels in white sitting where Jesus' body had been. Even in her sorrow, she was given a glimpse of the heavenly reality around her.
entries.20:13: The angels asked why she was crying, and she repeated her grief about not knowing where Jesus' body was. Her answer shows how completely focused her love for him was.
entries.20:14: Mary turned and saw Jesus standing there but didn't recognize him. Grief and assumptions can keep us from seeing what's right in front of us.
entries.20:15: Jesus asked Mary why she was crying and who she was looking for, and she mistook him for the gardener. She was so fixed on finding a body that she missed the living person speaking to her.
entries.20:16: Jesus simply said her name, and Mary instantly recognized him. Being known and called by name is deeply personal, and it opened her eyes.
entries.20:17: Jesus told Mary not to cling to him but to go tell his disciples that he was returning to the Father. He gave her a mission, and he made clear that his relationship with the Father is now shared with his followers.
entries.20:18: Mary went and told the disciples she had seen the Lord and passed on his message. She became the first witness of the resurrection, trusted with good news to share.
entries.20:19: That evening Jesus came to the disciples even though they were hiding behind locked doors for fear. His first words were a greeting of peace, meeting their fear with calm.
entries.20:20: Jesus showed them his hands and side so they could see he was really alive and really himself. The disciples were filled with joy when they saw him.
entries.20:21: Jesus again gave them peace and then sent them out just as the Father had sent him. His peace comes with a purpose, and his followers are given a mission.
entries.20:22: Jesus breathed on them and told them to receive the Holy Spirit. This gave them the power and presence of God to carry out the mission he'd just given them.
entries.20:23: Jesus gave his followers authority to declare forgiveness or to withhold it. This means the church carries real responsibility in announcing God's forgiveness to people.
entries.20:24: Thomas, one of the twelve, wasn't there when Jesus appeared. Being absent from the community meant he missed the first encounter with the risen Lord.
entries.20:25: The other disciples told Thomas they'd seen the Lord, but he refused to believe unless he could touch the wounds himself. His doubt was honest and specific, and he wasn't afraid to say what he needed.
entries.20:26: A week later Jesus came again through locked doors and stood among them with a greeting of peace, and this time Thomas was there. Jesus made a point of coming back for the one who had doubted.
entries.20:27: Jesus invited Thomas to touch his hands and side and to stop doubting and believe. He didn't scold Thomas but gave him exactly the evidence he'd asked for.
entries.20:28: Thomas responded by calling Jesus his Lord and his God. His doubt turned into one of the clearest declarations of who Jesus is in the whole Bible.
entries.20:29: Jesus said Thomas believed because he saw, but he blessed those who believe without seeing. That blessing includes everyone who trusts in Jesus today without having been there.
entries.20:30: Jesus did many other miraculous signs that aren't written down in this book. The Gospel doesn't claim to record everything, just what's needed.
entries.20:31: The accounts were written so readers would believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life through him. The whole point of the book is to bring you to faith and to life.
entries.21:1: Jesus showed himself to his disciples again, this time by a lake. It reminds the reader that Jesus can appear in ordinary places and moments.
entries.21:2: Seven of the disciples were gathered together by name. It shows that Jesus' followers were real, ordinary people who stayed together after his death.
entries.21:3: Peter decided to go back to his old job of fishing, and the others joined him, but they caught nothing all night. It shows that going back to normal life without Jesus' help can leave us empty.
entries.21:4: Jesus stood on the shore early in the morning, but the disciples did not recognize him. It reminds the reader that Jesus is often near us even when we don't notice him.
entries.21:5: Jesus called out to ask if they had caught anything, and they said no. It shows Jesus starting a conversation with people in their everyday failure.
entries.21:6: Jesus told them to try the other side of the boat, and suddenly they caught so many fish they could hardly pull the net in. It shows that obeying Jesus' simple word can turn an empty effort into abundance.
entries.21:7: The disciple closest to Jesus recognized him first and told Peter, who quickly jumped into the water to get to him. It shows that love for Jesus can make a person act boldly and eagerly.
entries.21:8: The other disciples followed in the boat, dragging the heavy net of fish a short distance to shore. It shows they worked together to bring in what Jesus had given them.
entries.21:9: When they reached land, they found Jesus had already made a fire with fish and bread ready. It shows Jesus caring for their practical needs before they even asked.
entries.21:10: Jesus told them to bring some of the fish they had just caught. It shows he invites people to share in what he is doing rather than doing everything for them.
entries.21:11: Peter dragged the net ashore full of 153 large fish, and the net did not break. It shows that Jesus' provision is generous and holds together under pressure.
entries.21:12: Jesus invited them to eat, and the disciples were too awed to ask who he was because they knew it was him. It shows that being near the risen Jesus can leave us silent with wonder.
entries.21:13: Jesus served them bread and fish himself. It shows Jesus as one who feeds and serves his followers rather than being served.
entries.21:14: This was the third time Jesus appeared to his disciples after rising from the dead. It reminds the reader that the resurrection was not a one-time rumor but something witnessed repeatedly.
entries.21:15: After the meal, Jesus asked Peter three times about his love and told him to feed his lambs. It shows that Jesus restores someone who failed him and gives them a job to care for others.
entries.21:16: Jesus asked Peter again if he loved him, and Peter said yes, so Jesus told him to care for his sheep. It shows that love for Jesus is shown by looking after the people he cares about.
entries.21:17: Jesus asked a third time, which hurt Peter, but Peter appealed to Jesus' knowledge of everything and said he loved him, and Jesus told him to feed his sheep. It shows Jesus gently healing Peter's past denials and trusting him again.
entries.21:18: Jesus told Peter that when he was young he went where he wanted, but when old he would be led where he did not want to go. It shows that following Jesus can cost us control over our own lives.
entries.21:19: Jesus said this to show what kind of death Peter would face, and then simply told him to follow. It shows that Jesus is honest about hard things ahead and still calls us to follow him.
entries.21:20: Peter turned and saw the disciple Jesus loved following them, the one who had leaned close at the last meal. It sets up Peter comparing his path with someone else's.
entries.21:21: Peter asked Jesus what would happen to that other disciple. It shows how easily we get distracted by other people's futures instead of our own calling.
entries.21:22: Jesus told Peter that what he wanted for the other disciple was none of Peter's business, and repeated the call to follow him. It shows that each person's job is to follow Jesus, not to manage everyone else's path.
entries.21:23: A rumor spread that this disciple would not die, but Jesus had not actually said that; he had only said it was his choice to make. It shows how easily words get twisted and how careful we should be with what Jesus actually said.
entries.21:24: This is the disciple who testified and wrote these things down, and the community affirms that his testimony is true. It gives the reader confidence that this account comes from a real eyewitness.
entries.21:25: Jesus did so many other things that, if all were written down, the writer thinks the world could not hold the books. It shows that the Gospels give us enough to believe, not everything there is to know.
